cards.title: Use Rejection-Then-Retreat to Raise Offer Acceptance
cards.summary: Make a larger request first and retreat to your real target offer so buyers accept more often and feel they dictated the deal.
cards.use_when: Pricing, bundles, or upsell decisions where you need a higher acceptance rate on a target offer (e.g., checkout upsell, extended warranty, bundle tier).

cards.title: Rejection-Then-Retreat Example: Service Contract Upsell
cards.summary: A TV/stereo salesperson pitched the longest, priciest service contract first, then retreated to a one-year plan, beating peers on contract attach.
cards.use_when: Designing an extended-warranty or protection-plan upsell at checkout, or training whoever writes your post-purchase offer.

cards.title: Defuse a Manipulative 'Free' Offer in Sourcing or Vendor Deals
cards.summary: Redefine a vendor's free gift, sample, or concession as a sales device so you can evaluate the paid offer on merit.
cards.use_when: Vendor or supplier negotiations (white-label samples, 'free' audits, free onboarding) where a gift precedes a purchase ask.

cards.title: Foot-in-the-Door: Convert Browsers with a Tiny First Commitment
cards.summary: A small first yes reliably raises later compliance with bigger asks, because people act to stay consistent with their new self-image.
cards.use_when: Email capture, account creation, or subscription steps where you want the first click to lead to a larger action (first purchase, plan upgrade).

cards.title: Small-Order 'Customer' Conversion: Turn Prospects into Buyers
cards.summary: A trivial first purchase converts a prospect into a customer in their own mind, making larger follow-on purchases natural.
cards.use_when: Product selection and offer design for first-purchase incentives, sample kits, or trial SKUs.

cards.title: Opening-Rapport Question That Increases Purchase Agreement
cards.summary: Asking callers 'How are you doing?' and having them say 'fine' roughly doubled agreement and drove near-universal purchase at the home visit.
cards.use_when: Cold calls, chat openers, or live-selling scripts where you want a first verbal commitment before a purchase ask.

cards.title: Why Buyers Justify Purchases: Consistency After Commitment
cards.summary: Once a buyer takes a stand (a ticket, an order), they shift beliefs to match the decision, becoming more confident and more likely to defend it.
cards.use_when: Retention and post-purchase decisions — reviews, referral asks, renewal messaging, upselling shortly after purchase.

cards.title: Beware the 'You Promised' Trap in Promo Scheduling
cards.summary: Undersupplying a promoted hero item can lock parents into a promise that drives substitute purchases now and the promised item later — as a customer, avoid being caught; as a merchant, know the pattern.
cards.use_when: Product selection and promo planning for seasonal launches, pre-orders, or limited-edition drops.

cards.title: Use optional purchase-intent questions to guide relevant follow-up
cards.summary: Treat stated product interest as a hypothesis for merchandising and follow-up, not a guaranteed commitment.
cards.use_when: Testing an optional product-interest survey before a launch or back-in-stock notification.

cards.title: Use optional customer goals to personalize product onboarding
cards.summary: Let customers state a useful product goal without creating pressure or cancellation friction.
cards.use_when: Onboarding forms, sign-up flows, cancellation saves, or warranty registration — anywhere you can ethically get the customer to write or type a commitment.

cards.title: Start Small and Build: Layered Commitment Sequence
cards.summary: Escalating from mild, easy agreements to harder requests works because each step makes the person act consistently with the prior one.
cards.use_when: Multi-touch acquisition or loyalty programs where you sequence micro-yes steps toward a larger commitment.

cards.title: Self-Image Is the Lever: Frame Offers Around Identity
cards.summary: People act to match their self-image, so getting a customer to see themselves as a certain kind of buyer drives more consistent subsequent behavior.
cards.use_when: Brand positioning, PDP/landing page copy, and loyalty messaging.

cards.title: Reconcile a Bad Review with a Buyer's Consistency Trap
cards.summary: Customers who have committed (bought, paid, signed up) may reject evidence that the purchase was wrong, even when they understand the counter-argument.
cards.use_when: Handling negative reviews, refund friction, or pre-purchase objections on PDPs and landing pages.

cards.title: Use voluntary written product goals in post-purchase onboarding
cards.summary: A self-chosen written commitment can make a product-use intention easier to revisit.
cards.use_when: Customers buy a product that requires a routine or learning period.

cards.title: Record independent judgments before debating ecommerce decisions
cards.summary: Publicly defending an initial position can make it harder to update when new evidence appears.
cards.use_when: A team is selecting products, creative concepts or experiment winners.

cards.title: Treat praise-contest submissions as selected marketing material
cards.summary: A contest asking people to praise a product selects and encourages favorable accounts; it is not an unbiased satisfaction survey.
cards.use_when: A brand collects customer essays or promotional testimonials.

cards.title: Separate effort invested from the value of a commerce project
cards.summary: Effort justification can cause teams to overvalue something because it was difficult to create.
cards.use_when: A costly launch, loyalty program or site redesign is under review.

cards.title: Distinguish reward-driven purchases from durable product preference
cards.summary: Behavior maintained by a strong external reward may not persist when that reward ends.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a discounted trial or loyalty incentive.

cards.title: Audit checkout for lowball pricing after customer commitment
cards.summary: Customers may rationalize staying after an attractive initial deal worsens; conversion alone does not justify hidden fees.
cards.use_when: Reviewing advertised offers and checkout totals.

cards.title: Keep public product-use commitments optional
cards.summary: Public commitments can support follow-through while also making people reluctant to change their minds.
cards.use_when: Designing a customer challenge or community program.

cards.title: Test retention after a clearly disclosed introductory incentive ends
cards.summary: Measure whether product value sustains repeat purchase once an explicitly limited introductory offer expires.
cards.use_when: Designing subscription trials, loyalty programmes, replenishment reminders or onboarding incentives where you plan to remove the discount/perk later.

cards.title: Public commitment to a behaviour predicts follow-through
cards.summary: People who agree to a behaviour and know it will be made public follow through far more than those who only receive information and a request.
cards.use_when: Designing referral programmes, review requests, sustainability claims, or community challenges where you want customers to act on a stated intention.

cards.title: Defend against consistency traps: use the stomach signal
cards.summary: When a request feels wrong but you feel cornered by something you already said or did, that physical unease is the signal to stop and name the trap.
cards.use_when: Negotiating supplier terms, reviewing a retargeting or upsell script, or evaluating any pitch that leverages your or your team's prior statements.

cards.title: The time-travel question to test whether a preference is real
cards.summary: Ask 'Knowing what I now know, if I could go back in time, would I make the same choice?' and trust the first flash of feeling before reasoning kicks in.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to discontinue a product line, keep a supplier, renew a partnership or trust a customer-research finding that may be self-justification.

cards.title: Social proof: people infer what is correct from what others do
cards.summary: We determine correct behaviour by observing others, so visible evidence of others acting is a shortcut that works even when the evidence is obviously fabricated.
cards.use_when: Designing PDP social proof, review widgets, bestseller badges, waitlists or community pages.

cards.title: Social proof is strongest under uncertainty
cards.summary: When customers are unsure or the situation is ambiguous, they rely most heavily on others' actions to decide.
cards.use_when: Merchandising unfamiliar categories, new-product launches, or high-consideration purchases where the customer has no prior experience.

cards.title: Bystander inaction and pluralistic ignorance
cards.summary: In ambiguous emergencies, everyone looks to everyone else for a cue that action is needed, so no one acts — a pattern relevant to how customers interpret vague signals.
cards.use_when: Designing support escalation, complaint handling, restock/availability messaging, or any page where the customer must decide whether their situation warrants action.

cards.title: Canned laughter: a partial cue can substitute for the real thing
cards.summary: A single disembodied feature of a real response (a laugh track, a count of buyers) can trigger the same automatic response as the genuine article.
cards.use_when: Auditing which proof elements on a PDP or landing page are substantive versus purely superficial cues.

cards.title: Validate product outcomes independently of enthusiastic community feedback
cards.summary: Separate committed-fan enthusiasm from evidence that the product delivers its promised result.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why churned or disappointed customers defend a product publicly, or managing community narrative after a failed launch or product miss.

cards.title: Identify the cost of a commitment before trying to reverse it
cards.summary: Commitments that cost the person something real — quitting a job, burning bridges, giving up possessions — generate the strongest resistance to admitting error.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much sunk cost to write off on a failed product line, inventory bet or marketing channel; and when interpreting customer or team resistance.

cards.title: People comply more with requests made by attractive, high-status requesters
cards.summary: The source's opening example shows a request framed as a survey succeeding because the requester's appearance and authority produced exaggerated cooperation.
cards.use_when: Designing who delivers your outreach — affiliate creators, live-shopping hosts, sales agents, or review creators.

cards.title: Make genuine early customer participation visible at launch
cards.summary: Display verified participation rather than manufactured popularity.
cards.use_when: Structuring live commerce streams, launch pages, donation-style or pre-order mechanics, and early-access programmes.

cards.title: Model behaviour reduces fear and changes action, including filmed examples
cards.summary: Watching a variety of others like themselves act overcomes hesitation; one exposure can produce lasting behaviour change.
cards.use_when: Designing demo videos, customer-story content, or tutorials for customers hesitant about an unfamiliar product or category.

cards.title: The 5%/95% rule: actions persuade more than arguments
cards.summary: Sales consultant Cavett Robert's claim, quoted by Cialdini, is that people are moved more by others' actions than by any proof you can offer.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much landing-page copy versus behavioural evidence to produce for a product launch.

cards.title: Use social proof ethically: the difference between cue and substance
cards.summary: The source distinguishes using others' behaviour as legitimate guidance from responding to patently fraudulent cues — and treats the latter as fraud, not cleverness.
cards.use_when: Setting policy for review moderation, influencer seeding, countdown/scarcity displays, and any 'X people bought this' widget.

cards.title: Prepare for disconfirmation: measure outcomes, not enthusiasm
cards.summary: The cult case shows that the more public and costly the commitment, the less members could tolerate its failure — a warning for reading hype as signal.
cards.use_when: Post-launch reviews, deciding whether to double down on a viral product or campaign, and interpreting community sentiment.

cards.title: Map the Low-Information Purchase to Social Proof Mechanics
cards.summary: Bystander research shows the persuasion job shifts from 'do they want it' to 'is this a real need and is it my job to act' — a map for low-information ecommerce traffic.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why traffic converts poorly on a novel or high-consideration product where visitors don't understand the category, or designing PDP content for cold traffic from social ads.

cards.title: Direct the Ask to One Person, Not the Crowd
cards.summary: Cialdini's key rule: a request directed at an individual converts far better than a general appeal to everyone, because it assigns responsibility and specifies the action.
cards.use_when: Writing CTAs, email copy, abandoned-cart messages, or exit-intent offers where the ask is currently generic ('Shop now', 'Learn more').

cards.title: Similarity Beats Authority in Social Proof Selection
cards.summary: Across wallet-return, antismoking, dental-anxiety and imitation research, people copy the similar other far more than the impressive one.
cards.use_when: Choosing which testimonials, reviews, creators or case studies to feature on a PDP, ad creative or landing page.

cards.title: When to Distrust Social Proof: Falsified and Uncertain Data
cards.summary: Cialdini's two failure modes for social proof are manufactured evidence and ambiguous situations — a two-question filter for reading any proof signal.
cards.use_when: Auditing existing reviews, badges, urgency widgets and 'bestseller' claims, or before trusting a competitor's visible proof as real demand.

cards.title: Lone Decision Time: Use Own Experience as the Backup Signal
cards.summary: Cialdini's closing defense: since social proof mostly helps but fails on fabricated inputs, keep it installed and learn to spot when to disengage.
cards.use_when: Setting a personal or team rule for when to distrust aggregate signals — best-seller lists, 'trending' labels, category hype — in assortment and buying decisions.

cards.title: Design the First Movers: Seed Visible Behavior in the Order You Want
cards.summary: Cialdini's reading of Jonestown: leaders don't persuade everyone, they arrange conditions so an initial visible minority's behavior persuades the rest.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product, category or community feature where the store needs to bootstrap visible purchase or usage behavior without faking it.

cards.title: Detect and Neutralize Fake Social Proof in Reviews and Testimonials
cards.summary: Spot counterfeit social evidence (staged testimonials, fake reviews, biased samples) and decide how to respond as a buyer and as an operator.
cards.use_when: Auditing supplier or marketplace reviews, or judging whether a competitor's or affiliate's social proof is trustworthy before you cite or copy it.

cards.title: Watch for Innocent Snowballing Social Proof (Nobody Actually Knows)
cards.summary: Crowd behavior can be wrong when each person is only copying the previous person, not acting on superior information.
cards.use_when: Interpreting demand signals, trending products, or 'everyone is buying this' momentum before you commit inventory or ad spend.

cards.title: Verify early marketplace momentum before treating it as durable demand
cards.summary: Treat ranking and trending signals as potentially self-reinforcing rather than proof of product quality.
cards.use_when: Evaluating bestseller badges, 'trending' indicators, or early-sales momentum as demand signals for product selection and inventory bets.

cards.title: Use Familiarity to Build Liking for Products and Brands
cards.summary: Repeated exposure produces liking, sometimes unconsciously, and familiarity can sway choices as large as voting.
cards.use_when: Planning repeat ad exposure, retargeting cadence, or building familiarity for a new brand or product before expecting conversion.

cards.title: When Familiarity Backfires: Contact Under Competition Creates Hostility
cards.summary: Repeated exposure only increases liking under pleasant conditions; under rivalry it breeds hostility, as seen in competitive classrooms.
cards.use_when: Designing any repeated-contact touchpoint (community, loyalty programs, supplier relations) where participants might see each other as rivals.

cards.title: Use Common Goals and 'Jigsaw' Interdependence to Build Liking
cards.summary: Cooperation toward shared goals overrides rivalry; the jigsaw structure makes each member's contribution necessary to everyone's success.
cards.use_when: Structuring cross-team, partner, or customer-community work where people from different groups must collaborate.

cards.title: The Tupperware Party Model: Make the Request Come From a Friend
cards.summary: Home-party sales convert because the psychologically compelling requester is a friend/hostess, not the unknown demonstrator.
cards.use_when: Designing referral programs, influencer or host/ambassador programs, or bundled events where customers sell to peers.

cards.title: Let customers initiate genuine ecommerce referrals
cards.summary: Use real relationships through customer-controlled sharing instead of collecting friends' contact lists.
cards.use_when: Building referral, ambassador or outbound-partnership programs where you approach prospects your customers already know.

cards.title: Joe Girard's Formula: A Fair Price Plus Someone They Like
cards.summary: A relentless top car salesman attributed his success to two simple ingredients: a fair price and someone the buyer liked.
cards.use_when: Designing sales-person or live-chat interactions, showroom experiences, or evaluating why a competitor's staff out-converts yours at similar prices.

cards.title: Physical Attractiveness as a Halo Effect in Buying and Hiring Decisions
cards.summary: Good looks trigger automatic favorable judgments — talent, honesty, intelligence — and measurably affect votes, hiring and even court outcomes.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to present people (founders, hosts, models, customer service) in PDPs, video, ads and live selling, and auditing your own evaluation bias in hiring.

cards.title: Similarity Sells: Matching Dress, Background and Style to Increase Compliance
cards.summary: People comply more with those who seem similar in opinions, background or style, and small or even claimed similarities work.
cards.use_when: Training sales or support staff, writing outreach, or matching creative to an audience segment for conversion.

cards.title: Use sincere customer appreciation in postpurchase touchpoints
cards.summary: Test simple appreciation that reflects the real customer relationship.
cards.use_when: Designing customer touchpoints, thank-you notes, post-purchase messages or sales scripts where you want to build liking.

cards.title: Cooperation as a Liking Trigger — and 'We're on the Same Side' in Sales
cards.summary: Compliance professionals manufacture or amplify cooperation to make buyers feel they share goals, as when a salesperson 'battles' the boss on the buyer's behalf.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to use 'I'll fight for you' negotiation framing with buyers, or addressing where a customer perceives you as an adversary.

cards.title: The Four Liking Levers and How to Test Them in Store Touchpoints
cards.summary: Cialdini identifies physical attractiveness, similarity, compliments, familiarity and cooperation as the reliable causes of liking, each exploited by professionals.
cards.use_when: Building a checklist for live selling, chat, community or creative work when conversion lags behind price competitiveness.

cards.title: Show how the store helps with a real customer constraint
cards.summary: Explain genuine customer advocacy without staged conflict or invented enemies.
cards.use_when: Writing sales copy, chat scripts, or live-selling patter where you need to convert a hesitant buyer, or training CS/sales staff on how to position your company against a frustrating third party.

cards.title: Association Principle: Pair Products With Liked Elements, Unconsciously
cards.summary: Liking transfers by mere co-occurrence — attractive models, celebrities, and cultural moments change how people rate a product without them noticing.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative, influencer partnerships, lifestyle imagery, or brand sponsorships where the goal is to shift product perception.

cards.title: Bad News Infects the Teller: Keep the Brand Off the Blame Path
cards.summary: People dislike whoever delivers unpleasant information even when that person is not responsible — so never let your brand be the visible face of bad news.
cards.use_when: Writing emails about price increases, stockouts, shipping delays, order problems, or returns; designing who delivers bad news across support and lifecycle messaging.

cards.title: The Luncheon Technique: Attach Positive Feelings via Food or Pleasure Adjacent to Your Message
cards.summary: Positive feelings become attached to whatever is experienced while eating or otherwise enjoying something — a lever for event selling, sampling, and branded moments.
cards.use_when: Planning pop-up shops, trade-show booths, tasting events, VIP dinners, in-person demos, or any content where you want product judgments to shift favorably.

cards.title: Basking in Reflected Glory: Sell Identity, Not Just Product
cards.summary: Customers publicly display connections to winners and hide connections to losers, especially when their own image is damaged — identity and belonging drive purchase and display behavior.
cards.use_when: Building brand community, merch and logo-wear strategy, creator or team partnerships, and content promising self-image improvement.

cards.title: Defense Against Liking: Detect Undue Liking, Then Separate the Person From the Deal
cards.summary: You cannot block every liking tactic, so instead let them work and monitor one thing — whether you like this counterpart more than the circumstances warrant.
cards.use_when: Negotiating with suppliers, agencies, affiliate partners, marketplace reps or salespeople where personal rapport may be overriding commercial judgment.

cards.title: Reciprocity Pressure Can Force a Commitment: Watch for Borrowed-Relationship Bundles
cards.summary: The MCI Calling Circle case shows that making a customer's switch a favor to a friend converts better than any feature pitch — and that this pressure is a real, exploitable lever.
cards.use_when: Designing referral programs, subscription switches, group or family plans, or any offer that routes through an existing customer's social circle.

cards.title: Authority Deference Is Extreme: Don't Assume Customers Resist Expert Framing
cards.summary: Milgram's subjects delivered what they believed were painful shocks on a lab-coated researcher's word — evidence that legitimate-looking authority overrides personal judgment far more than people predict.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much credibility signaling (credentials, expert endorsements, certifications, clinical or engineering spokespeople) to place on a PDP or landing page.

cards.title: Authority Persuasion in Ecommerce: Defense Checklist
cards.summary: Two questions—is this a true expert, and how truthful is the expert here—help shoppers and operators resist automatic deference triggered by titles, uniforms and trappings.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to follow an 'expert' recommendation that affects merchandising, pricing, fulfillment or store policy, or when auditing your own site's claims for credibility.

cards.title: Recognize When Authority Symbols Replace Real Credentials
cards.summary: Titles, clothing and expensive trappings trigger compliance even without genuine expertise, so shoppers and operators should separate symbol from substance.
cards.use_when: Merchandising or creating content where authority-like signals (badges, uniforms, expert imagery, luxury cues) are used, and when assessing competitor claims or negotiating with suppliers.

cards.title: Use Scarcity Framing to Increase Willingness to Buy
cards.summary: Framing offers around potential loss rather than gain tends to motivate more action, because scarcity makes the same item feel more valuable.
cards.use_when: Writing product page copy, email subject lines or ad creative for a limited stock, seasonal or discontinued item.

cards.title: Use truthful low-stock and back-in-stock flows
cards.summary: Communicate actual availability while letting shoppers choose whether to wait.
cards.use_when: Launching limited drops, managing low-stock SKUs, or designing recovery messaging for out-of-stock items.

cards.title: Deadline Pressure: Shrinking Opportunity Window
cards.summary: Deadlines make people act on opportunities they otherwise would ignore, because the time to get something is running out.
cards.use_when: Planning flash sales, launch windows, enrollment periods for subscriptions or membership tiers, or limited-time bundles.

cards.title: Scarcity Raises Perceived Value, Even for Flawed Items
cards.summary: Rare or becoming-rare items are judged more valuable, and even flaws become prized when tied to scarcity.
cards.use_when: Positioning limited editions, discontinued lines, archive or vintage inventory, and setting prices for rare stock.

cards.title: Detecting the Self-Interest Disguise in Vendor and Partner Pitches
cards.summary: When someone argues against their own interest on a small point, it can be a credibility move designed to make a bigger ask land.
cards.use_when: Negotiating with suppliers, agencies, platforms or marketplace partners, and when writing your own sales or upsell copy.

cards.title: Apply the Precious-Error Defense to Product Claims and Specs
cards.summary: Because authority pressure makes people stop thinking once a legitimate authority has spoken, errors and misleading claims can pass unchallenged through store operations.
cards.use_when: Reviewing product listings, subscription terms, dosages, compatibility claims or return policies before publishing.

cards.title: Expect Underestimated Authority Effects in Customer Research
cards.summary: People consistently misjudge how much authority cues will influence them, so self-reported intent underestimates real compliance.
cards.use_when: Interpreting survey or concept-test feedback on authority-based design (expert endorsements, uniforms, premium branding) or deciding whether to A/B test instead.

cards.title: Resolve product-fit concerns before offering an add-on
cards.summary: An honest useful recommendation may build trust before a relevant complementary offer.
cards.use_when: Designing upsell, bundle or add-on flows in cart and checkout.

cards.title: Establish a Verification Habit Against Authority Shortcuts
cards.summary: Since authority prompts click-whirr compliance, embed lightweight verification steps rather than relying on vigilance in the moment.
cards.use_when: Setting store operations for supplier approvals, pricing decisions, creative review or claims sign-off.

cards.title: Scarcity and deadline tactics in merchandising
cards.summary: How limited-number and deadline pressure tactics work in retail, and when they are legitimate vs manipulative.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a limited-stock or time-limited promotion on a PDP, landing page, or campaign.

cards.title: Newly scarce beats always scarce
cards.summary: The drop from abundance to scarcity increases desire more than constant scarcity, so change-of-availability moments outperform permanent limits.
cards.use_when: Choosing how to frame a promotion, restock, or last-chance message on a product page or email.

cards.title: Test genuine demand signals alongside inventory availability
cards.summary: Observed demand can add context to low stock, but its effect on ecommerce purchasing needs testing.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, drop announcements, or sale creative where multiple buyers are chasing limited stock.

cards.title: Using arousal as your own spending signal
cards.summary: Because scarcity suppresses rational thought, the visceral feeling of urgency is the cue to pause before buying, not a reason to buy.
cards.use_when: Managing your own procurement, ad-buying, or inventory purchasing decisions under competitive pressure.

cards.title: Scarcity of information is persuasive (exclusive intelligence)
cards.summary: Information believed to be exclusive is more persuasive than the same information framed as common knowledge, so make genuinely proprietary insight the centerpiece of offers.
cards.use_when: Crafting B2B wholesale pitches, trade communications, or any pitch where supply/price news is the selling point.
